claim: Left alone, people and LLMs mostly pick tests that fit their hypothesis (positive test bias); programming experience does not fix it. In a 2019 software-testing experiment 86.5% of 371 student test cases were spec-consistent (confirmatory), with or without time pressure.
agent_test: Run the agent on 2-4-6 style rule tasks and on code-fix tasks; log share of tests that could fail the current answer; compare schema with and without a forced 'break it' test at equal tokens.

claim: A prompt that asks for tests that would break the hypothesis (Think-in-Opposites, Dual-Goal) raises rule-discovery success. Humans, randomised N=180: 78.3% vs 36.7% control (properties-only training 38.3%). LLMs: 42% to 56% on average, infirming-to-confirming test ratio up in 18 of 22 cases. Shown on 2-4-6 rule games only; not shown on real code fixes (see K23).
agent_test: Add one 'name a test that would falsify this' line at S4 and measure fail-detection on seeded wrong solutions at equal tokens.

claim: Models that use fewer positive tests win more hidden-rule games (Spearman rho -0.779 success vs positive-test rate; 12 models x 100 games); the same direction holds inside the Failing to Falsify study.
agent_test: Correlate per-run share of falsifying tests with final correctness in our own logs.

claim: Tests written from a spec or rule list beat tests that probe edges freely or see the buggy code. Zhao 2026 (Java Defects4J): effective bug-finding tests 104 to 187 per model (230 advanced prompt); 15-21% of docstrings inherited the bug. Haeri 2026 (Python, Claude Haiku/Sonnet/Opus, GPT-5.3-codex, Gemini 3.5 Flash): final correct code 62% to 100% (+38 pp) with rule-grounded tests, 0% vs 33% false alarms. Gap vanishes on well-specified algorithmic tasks (HumanEval+). Neither study compares code-visible vs code-hidden with everything else fixed.
agent_test: S4: generate tests from the problem statement in a context that never contains the candidate code; compare with tests written with code visible.

claim: Weak test sets let wrong code pass: 80x more tests drop pass@1 by up to 19.3% across 26 models; LLM-written tests also cluster on happy paths (null 34.8%, negative 23.8% coverage).
agent_test: Evaluate agent answers against extended and mutated inputs, not only the given examples; report the pass drop.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Self-review without an external signal does not help and often hurts (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0 after two rounds); oracle feedback helps; self-repair gains vanish at matched compute.
agent_test: Compare revise-by-self-critique with revise-only-on-code-failure at equal tokens.

claim: Anchoring on prior in-context material is the strongest and most robust LLM bias: Codex copies wrong anchor-function lines in 32-61% of solutions; irrelevant framing lines appear in 81% of outputs; numeric anchors move GPT-3 and GPT-3.5 like humans; mean anchoring score 0.39 over 20 models; 22-61% of SynAnchors questions anchored. PROBE-SWE found anchoring the weakest (5.9%), so SE-vignette anchoring is smaller.
agent_test: Retry a failed task with (a) the failed attempt in context, (b) the failed attempt removed; compare pass rate at equal tokens.

claim: Instructions to ignore or be careful about an anchor do not cancel it: obsolete requirements still raised human estimates in 6 of 6 experiments; LLM warning prompts moved median SE bias sensitivity only 12.9% to 10.3%, and some prompts made anchoring worse.
agent_test: Compare 'ignore X' versus physically removing X from the context.

claim: A short awareness workshop reduces but does not remove anchoring in professionals (workshop effect on estimates d=0.72 against anchor effect d=1.19; variance threefold lower); the design is non-randomised across series.
agent_test: Measure residual anchoring after a bias warning in the system prompt, as a dose check only.

claim: Chain-of-thought and extra thinking budget do not reliably reduce bias: zero-shot CoT raised SE bias sensitivity (12.9% to 16.1%); reasoning models were not less biased than siblings (+0.031, p=.157); AnchorBench CoT lowered plausible-anchor influence in 11 of 15 cells (mean -0.06) but left it above zero in 13 of 15 and raised it in 4; bias grows with task complexity (confirmation +33.7 pp per tier).
agent_test: Vary thinking budget at a fixed schema; track anchoring and confirmation scores. Contested because SynAnchors found reasoning models least anchored.

claim: Reasoning models anchor less on SynAnchors (22.0-25.0% vs up to 60.5% for small models), which conflicts with Kraishan's null difference between reasoning and non-reasoning siblings.
agent_test: Run both bias probes on our chosen base model with thinking on and off.

claim: Writing out the rule a correct answer must satisfy before answering cuts measured bias: PROBE-SWE axiomatic cues about 51% (12.9% to 6.3-7.5%, wide intervals, except hindsight); AnchorBench plausible-anchor index 0.33 to 0.06 with an explicit rule vs 0.26 with a vague 'weigh credibility' instruction. Works where a rule can be stated; generic 'be unbiased' prompts backfire on judgment biases (-4.4%, CogBias).
agent_test: At S1 have the agent list the checks a correct answer must pass, then test against them.

claim: Confirmation bias in LLM decision scenarios is model-dependent: mean score 0.15 over 20 models, range -0.18 to 0.72, and one test shows models leaning opposite to humans. Optimism, planning fallacy and escalation of commitment are near zero.
agent_test: Run the scenario confirmation probe on the chosen model before spending schema space on it.

claim: The 'logic training reduced confirmation bias' claim rests on one research group's correlational work (Calikli, Arslan, Bener 2010, N=88; companion PROMISE 2010 and SQJ 2015 papers). Students beat staff on abstract questions (chi2 8.114), but in the experience-matched comparison (43 vs 13) the only significant difference was test duration. No external replication and no randomised trial in software testers found. Non-software trials exist: Branchini 2025 randomised N=180 (78.3% vs 36.7%), Sellier 2019 quasi-experiment N=290 (58.8% vs 72.2% chose the confirming option).
agent_test: None needed: build falsification into the scaffold instead of relying on a trained skill.

claim: The link from confirmation bias to production defects is not statistically supported (5 developers, 12 testers, no significance test).
agent_test: n/a

claim: No debiasing technique in SE had strong empirical evidence as of 2016 (6 of 37 biases have any proposed technique).
agent_test: n/a; treat all human-derived fixes as hypotheses to measure.

claim: About half of developer actions with LLMs carry a bias (47-49%), higher for LLM actions (54-56%); fixation on the first suggestion leads to most reversals (43.4%); the bias-reversal link of the 2020 study did not replicate (p=0.058, reversal 25% vs 52.9%).
agent_test: Force a second independent candidate before testing; compare reversal rate with the single-candidate flow.

claim: Anchoring on task framing changes self-rated code comprehensibility (path 0.165; professionals as much as students) but not actual understanding performance (d=-0.006).
agent_test: Check whether 'this is easy' wording changes the agent's stated confidence versus its actual accuracy.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Many LLM 'bias' results may be prompt sensitivity or recognition of known quiz forms, not human-like bias; low bias scores can reflect failure to follow the task.
agent_test: Pair every bias score with task accuracy.

claim: Instruction tuning increases some biases (decoy, certainty, belief bias) and instruction-tuned models test positives most (66-82%).
agent_test: Compare base and instruct models on the falsification probe if both are available. a24 was read from abstract only.

claim: Content matters: LMs and humans do better on Wason-type logic when content matches belief, and poorly on abstract rules.
agent_test: Phrase falsification checks in abstract rule form versus story form. a22 and c22 are the same paper (arXiv 2207.07051).

claim: Self-debiasing by rewriting the prompt removes most biased cues for strong models (GPT-4 framing 2.7%, group attribution 0%) but weaker models flip decisions too often.
agent_test: Add a neutral restatement step at S0 and measure answer flips on paired biased/unbiased prompts.

claim: A failed attempt left in context anchors small code models: with the failed program shown, pass@1 fell 6.1 points (1.5B, p=0.006) and 6.9 points (3B, p<0.001) below a blind resample, near-identical retries rose from 2-14% to 33-68%, execution feedback added nothing over a content-free notice. For 30B+ models with real test feedback, self-repair matches or beats resampling and uses fewer tokens. No test on a frontier reasoning model.
agent_test: After a failed attempt, compare a retry with the failed code in context against a retry from the original task plus only the failing test; log similarity between attempts and pass rate at equal tokens.

claim: Software-specific human evidence for debiasing is absent: no randomised trial of logic or hypothesis-testing training on positive test bias in testers, and no external replication of Calikli et al. 2010. Nearest evidence is outside software (Branchini 2025 RCT on Wason task; Sellier 2019 field transfer).
agent_test: n/a; treat any training claim as a hypothesis to measure on the agent.

claim: Spec completeness moderates test quality: Leventhal 1994 reported positive test bias in all conditions, reduced by expertise and more complete specs (abstract only, not opened); Haeri 2026 found that dropping validation rules cut bug detection from 30/30 to 6/30 while tests stayed accurate, and that a wrong rule endorsing the bug lowered test accuracy to 82.8% without hiding the bug. Time pressure did not raise confirmatory testing (Salman 2019, d=-0.357, n.s.).
agent_test: Give the test writer a complete rule list vs a partial one and measure detection; add a rule that endorses a known bug and see if tests still catch it.

claim: Anchoring in LLMs depends on how the anchor reaches the model (external, history, RAG, tool, in-context example) and on whether a plausible anchor sits near the evidence; accuracy without anchors does not predict robustness (frontier API models above 95% control accuracy still shifted).
agent_test: Run the anchor probe through each pathway the scaffold uses (memory, retrieved notes, earlier answers) rather than only the prompt.

claim: Ordinary software effort estimates from LLMs move with request wording ('how many hours of work' vs 'how much can be done in Y hours'), with anchoring-like patterns in two of five replicated human experiments (abstract only; older models).
agent_test: Ask the agent for the same estimate under both request formats and compare.

claim: No study found that a reference-class base-rate request lowers an LLM's optimism about its own success. Frontier models already use stated base rates near-correctly on word problems (slopes near 1), and multi-estimate elicitation does not debias them.
agent_test: Compare the agent's stated success probability with and without a reference-class prompt against actual pass rate on held-out tasks.
